statement: Presale homes in Metro Vancouver made comparable: a dated deposit schedule, unit-by-unit comparison and a platform rating, free to buyers.
team: A single Figma file: 76 screens and a 261-component library
heroCaption: The buyer’s path on a phone: a property’s price band and key figures, one unit’s economics, and three units compared.

snapshot.problem: A presale buyer commits a staged deposit years before the home exists, and the numbers that decide it are rarely side by side.
snapshot.role: Product designer across seven responsive flows, 76 screens and a 261-component design system.
snapshot.result: A complete design record for the buyer’s side of a presale market, with no launch evidence on file.

context.heading: Conscious Choice
body: CProperty is a marketplace for presale homes — condos and townhouses sold before they are built — in British Columbia’s Lower Mainland. The C stands for conscious, and the hero line repeats it: “Choose Consciously, Invest Delightfully.” The sample addresses sit in Vancouver’s West End.

The market was briefed city by city in a note that sits in the file: Vancouver and the North Shore, the Tri-Cities, Burnaby, New Westminster, Surrey, Richmond, Langley, and an outer ring out to Abbotsford and White Rock. The design is one Figma file of 13 pages: seven product flows — home, property, developer, property list, units and floor plans, sign-in and blog — six of them drawn at desktop, tablet and mobile width and the blog at desktop and mobile, 76 screens in all, plus a design system and an archive of an earlier version.

problem.heading: A deposit on a building that isn’t built yet
body: A presale buyer commits money years before there is anything to walk through: a deposit paid in instalments during construction, an assignment fee if they need to sell the contract before completion, a monthly maintenance charge per square foot, and a delivery date years away. The numbers that decide the purchase usually live in different places — a developer’s brochure, a sales centre, a spreadsheet.
CProperty’s job is to put them side by side, for one project and then across units, so a buyer can see what a home costs before, during and after it is built.

pivot.heading: From brochures for realtors to comparisons for buyers
body: The file keeps an earlier version on its own page: 57 frames of a different product. It sold to realtors. A premium account came in two tiers — Starter at $150 a year and Enhanced at $250, or $50 and $75 for three months — and unlocked full data and pricing for each unit, side-by-side comparison, saved favourites and, on Enhanced, customised brochures for client presentations. Realtors had a dashboard with a proposal builder: pick units, a colour swatch and one of six brochure templates. Developers had screens to add projects and mark units available, reserved or sold out.

The redesign turns that around. The dashboards and tiers are gone, browsing is free, and intent arrives through two forms: Contact Sales Center under the unit table, and Get Exclusive Information on the property and developer pages, which asks whether the sender is a realtor or a buyer. Realtors are still served — as leads, not subscribers. The proposal builder’s core idea, putting units side by side, survives as the compare page, and it now compares money rather than specifications.

approach.heading: The file records its order of work
body: Figma node IDs grow as a file is edited, so each frame’s median ID orders the work. The earlier version and the design-system foundation arrived first, at set-up. Home and the property page followed, then the property list with its filters and the sign-in flow at about the same time, then the developer page. Units, unit details and compare were drawn last — the most decision-heavy part of the product.

Every flow is laid out the same way: a title card, then a column per breakpoint — desktop at 1,440, tablet at 1,028 and mobile at 360 or 393 — with one screen per state. A final pass swapped a new footer into nearly every screen on every page.

solution.heading: Filters that ask investment questions
body: The list page opens with “Invest Delightfully with Selecting Project!” and a filter bar that asks an investor’s questions first: location, delivery date, investment rate, deposit and price. Bedrooms, bathrooms, parking, storage, property type, maximum total deposit and completion date wait under Advanced. Each of the six filters is drawn open: a grid of city chips, a calendar, sliders for rate, deposit and price, and the advanced panel.

The property page reads like a presale checklist. Beside the gallery sit a price band and six figures — delivery year, deposit, investment rate, monthly payment, unit plan types and average rent. Below, the page runs from the overview through units and floor plans, a deposit schedule drawn as dated instalments, interior and exterior design with priced extras for storage and parking, and a house-value section with neighbourhood charts, to price and expenses: mortgage scenarios by down payment, monthly payments across interest rates, and the cash due at closing.

compare.heading: Compare units, not buildings
body: Units and floor plans are a table — project, floor plan, bedrooms plus flex, location, size, price — with a favourite, More and Add to Compare on every row, and a Contact Sales Center form underneath. Unit details repeat the economics for a single unit: price, delivery date, assignment fee, maintenance per square foot, down payment and plan.

The compare page lines up three units in the same order: economics first — total, assignment fee, maintenance, down payment — then amenities, living essentials such as parking and EV charging, residence essentials, and a CProperty Rating for interior design and house value. The rating turns the brand’s promise into a field: the platform grades the home, not only the listing.
compare.insight: Every unit carries a CProperty Rating, so each comparison ends with the platform’s own judgement.

critique.heading: Four deposits on one page
body: The sample property answers “how much do I pay before completion?” four different ways. The header says a 30% deposit. The info block says a $32,500 total deposit and a 25% down payment. The deposit schedule says 20% in total — and its instalments, 8%, 4%, 4% and 2%, add up to 18%.

The location filter has the same kind of gap. The market brief lists Langley, Burnaby, Coquitlam, Port Coquitlam and Port Moody among its cities; the filter’s fifteen chips leave out Langley and Port Coquitlam and show Coquitlam twice, while every sample unit in the desktop table is in Langley. The earlier version’s filter had included Langley, Port Coquitlam and Delta.
bullets: The price panel is labelled “Deposite” and reuses the deposit slider’s range.
Delivery date is picked from a single month of days, while the delivery years in the file run from 2024 to 2026.
Percentages are written with the sign first (%30), and “Deposite” is misspelt throughout.
critique.insight: The most important number on the page is the one it states least consistently.

system.heading: A 0.0.1 system in brown and cream
body: The design system is labelled version 0.0.1 across eleven boards: colour, typography, header and footer, buttons, checkboxes and radios, toggles, profile, modal, form fields, breadcrumbs and toasts. It holds 13 component sets with 248 variants — buttons alone account for 90 — and 67 colour styles. The brand ramps are a main brown and a cream; blue, grey, green and red carry state. An icon page adds 120 icon sets in five sizes, with boards of amenity and place icons.

Two gaps show where it stopped. There are no variables: the one variable collection is empty, so every colour is a style. And the type board documents Poppins and Mazzard, while most screens are set in Hurme Geometric Sans 3, which appears in only one of the 12 text styles.

decisions.heading: Five decisions behind the comparison
decisions.lede: The redesign rests on five choices the file makes visible.

items.title: Give buyers the numbers for free, and treat realtors as leads
items.why: The earlier version sold unit data, side-by-side comparison and client brochures to realtors on annual or three-month plans. The redesign opens those numbers to every visitor and routes intent through two forms, one of which asks whether the sender is a realtor or a buyer.
items.tradeoff: Revenue has to come from leads rather than subscriptions, and the file records no model for pricing them.

items.title: Show the deposit as a schedule, not a single percentage
items.why: A presale deposit is paid in dated instalments over the build, and a single figure hides when the money is due. The property page draws it as tiles, each with its share and its date.
items.tradeoff: Every project needs its schedule entered, and the total has to agree with the header — which, on the sample page, it doesn’t.

items.title: Compare units, not projects
items.why: Assignment fees, maintenance per square foot, and parking or EV-charging extras differ by unit and plan, so Add to Compare sits on every unit row and the compare page lines up three units’ economics.
items.tradeoff: More rows to maintain, and a compare page that grows long on a phone.

items.title: Put the platform’s own rating beside the listing data
items.why: The brand’s promise — a conscious choice — becomes a field: a CProperty Rating for interior design and house value on every unit and in every comparison.
items.tradeoff: A rating needs a published method to be trusted; the file shows the scores, not how they are made.

items.title: Filter by investment questions first
items.why: Location, delivery date, investment rate, deposit and price sit on the bar; bedrooms, bathrooms, parking and storage wait under Advanced. The buyer this bar imagines is deciding where to put money before choosing a floor plan.
items.tradeoff: A family searching by bedroom count has to open Advanced first.

items.title: One number, one source
items.body: The sample property states its deposit four ways. On a presale page the deposit is the number a buyer plans around; it should be stored once and rendered everywhere, so that a header and a schedule cannot disagree.

items.title: Check the build against the brief
items.body: The market brief named every city and neighbourhood; the location filter dropped two of them and doubled a third. Comparing the finished filter against the brief, line by line, would have caught it in minutes.

items.title: Document the type you actually use
items.body: The type board declares Poppins and Mazzard, while most screens are set in Hurme Geometric Sans 3, which appears in a single text style. A design system is only a system if it describes the screens it serves.
